title: Stellar shrapnel
caption: The supernova remnant DEM L71, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: DEM L71 · constellation Dorado · about 160000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Separate fiery filaments are scattered across this Hubble scene. They are the shrapnel of a star that exploded several thousand years ago, some 160 000 light-years away in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a galaxy close to our own. The remnant is called DEM L71.

The star that exploded was a white dwarf, the dense leftover core of a star. Most stars in the Milky Way with masses from a tenth of the Sun's up to eight times it are expected to end up this way. A white dwarf in a binary can siphon gas from a close companion. If it takes more than it can handle, it turns unstable and blows up in what is called a Type Ia supernova.

That is what happened to the star behind DEM L71. The white dwarf ripped itself apart, flinging out a superheated cloud of debris. As the debris slammed into the surrounding gas, it slowly spread into the filaments.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.68 x 2.00 arcminutes) and distance (160000 light years), the frame spans roughly 125 × 93 light-years. Its light set out about 160,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 imaged the remnant in visible and near-infrared light, including a hydrogen-alpha filter. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: These faint filaments, partly recorded in near-infrared light, would be invisible to the eye.

explore: Around 97% of stars in that mass range are expected to become white dwarfs. Before it blows up, the white dwarf is thought to grow until it is about half again as large as the Sun. Supernovae are among the brightest events ever observed.
alt: Scattered fiery filaments of material from an exploded star.
